Interview Guide 
Congratulations, You Got the Interview! 
Getting an i
nterview is a significant 
achievement. Your resume and cover letter 
have successfully showcased your qualifications, 
impressing the prospective employer enough to 
want to meet you in person (or virtually). Now, 
it's your chance to confirm your skills and 
abilities, demonstrate your fit for the role, and 
learn more about the role and the company. 
This interview is not only an opportunity for 
them to get to know you better but also for you 
to expand on your resume, present your 
strengths confidently, and evaluate if this 
position and organization are the right match 
for your career aspirations. Prepare well, stay 
positive, and make the most of this exciting 
opportunity – you’re already off to a great start! 
Top 10 Tips for a Successful Interview 
1. Understand the role: Know the key
responsibilities and skills required.
2. Research the company: Understand its
mission, values, and recent news. How do
your personal and professional values align
with the organization’s?
3. Prepare answers using the SOAR method to
possible questions (p9); share your stories -
experience, skills and accomplishments.
4. Anticipate responses to common questions.
5. Develop thoughtful questions about the role
and company.
6. Dress appropriately: Choose professional
attire.
7. Practice: Conduct mock interviews with CDC
career advisors. Record yourself using
technology.
8. Plan your journey: For in person interviews,
arrive early (10 min). If virtual, test
technology and set up (lighting/sound).
9. Bring doc
uments: Have resumes,
references, and a notepad.
10. Follow up: Send a thank-you email and
reflect on your performance.
DIFFERENT INTERVIEW TYPES & FORMATS
1. Pre-screening Interview (virtual/phone)
The first interview. Commonly used to pre-
screen applicants before an in-person interview
is scheduled or when the candidate and
employer are not located in the same city.
Telephone Interview tips 
• Find a quiet location: Minimize
background noise.
• Prepare notes: Have your key points
and resume at hand.
• Practice speaking clearly: Ensure clarity
and pace.
• Listen actively: Don’t interrupt and
respond thoughtfully.
• Smile: It reflects in your voice.
Video Interview tips 
• Test technology - ensure a stable Wi-Fi
connection, working camera and
microphone and fully charged device.
• Choose a quiet, well-lit space with a
professional background.
• Dress like you would for an in-person
interview.
• Maintain eye contact - look at the
camera, not the screen and remember
to smile.
• Prepare notes - have your key points
and resume at hand.
• Minimize distractions - silence
notifications.

TYPES OF INTERVIEW QUESTIONS
1. Behavioral Interview questions focus on how
the candidate has handled past situations. The
interviewer asks questions based on the
competencies required to do the job. These
questions assess your experience and are
based on the premise that past behavior is the
best predictor of future behavior.
Example: "Tell me about a time when you had
to lead a team under a tight deadline."
2. Situational Interview questions present
hypothetical situations that can occur on the job
and asks the applicant how they would handle
them. This type of interview question assesses
problem-solving and analytical skills.
Example: "What would you do if you were faced 
with an unhappy customer?" 
3. Techni
cal Interview questions assess specific
technical skills and knowledge related to the job.
Common in fields such as finance, actuary,
accounting, data analytics.
Example: "Can you explain the concept of 
discounted cash flow (DCF) analysis and walk 
me through how you would use it to value a 
company.” 
4. Case interview questions are a critical part of
the management consulting recruitment process.
The primary goal is to assess the candidate's
problem-solving skills, analytical abilities, and how
they would approach real-world business
challenges that a consultant might face.
Example: "A client’s sales have dropped by 20% 
over the past year. How would you investigate 
and address this issue?"

reviewing their website, following their social 
media, and connecting with people you may

roduce Yourself. Greet the interviewer

Handling the "What is Your Salary 
Expectation?" Question 
One of the most challenging questions in a job 
interview is "What is your salary expectation?" 
It's important to approach this question with 
careful consideration, research, and tact. Here 
are some steps and tips to help you navigate 
this question confidently and professionally. 
1. Do Your Research
Before going to the interview, spend time 
researching salary ranges for the position you 
are applying for. Consider the following 
resources: 
• Online Salary Databases: Websites like
Glassdoor, PayScale, and LinkedIn Salary
can provide a range of salaries for specific
job titles and geographic locations.
• The Asper Employment Report available on
the website.
• Industry Reports: Professional associations
and industry reports often publish salary
surveys.
• Network: Talk to people in the industry,
including mentors, career services, and
alumni, to get a sense of typical salaries.

Prepare Your Answer 
You generally want to defer answering the 
salary question until you receive a job offer. 
The longer you can postpone providing a range, 
the more leverage you will have when it comes 
time to negotiate your salary – ideally when the

candidate and has offered you the position.

have several options for framing your response:

finding a role that fits my skills and career
aspirations. I'm confident that if we
determine I'm the right fit, we can agree on

• Turn the Question Around: "I'm flexible and
open to negotiation. Can you share the
budgeted salary range for this position?"
• Provide a Range: "Based on my research
and considering my experience and skills, I
believe a salary range of $X to $Y would be
appropriate. However, I'm open to
discussing this further."

ident and Professional. Your delivery is

• Be Honest: Don’t inflate your expectations
unrealistically.
• Be Flexible: Show that you’re open to
negotiation.
• Be Positive: Frame your response in a way
that shows you’re motivated and interested
in the position and company.

more confident and reduce anxiety. Consider 
answering the salary question by role playing 
with friends, family, or career services staff to 
refine your answer.

Behaviour Descriptive Interview 
Questions & How to Answer 
Behavioural-based or behaviour descriptive 
interview questions are designed to assess your 
past behavior in specific situations to predict 
your future performance in similar scenarios, 
using required competencies. These questions 
typically start with phrases like "Tell me about a 
time when..." or "Give an example of..." and 
focus on power/soft skills such as teamwork, 
problem-solving, leadership, and adaptability. 
Why Employers Use Behavioral-Based 
Interview Questions 
• To Predict Future Performance: Past
behavior is considered a reliable indicator of
future actions.
• To Evaluate Experience: Employers can
understand better how you have handled
real-life situations.
• To Assess Soft Skills: BDI questions help
interviewers gauge soft skills that are crucial
for job performance but not easily
measurable through technical questions.
How to Answer Behavioral-Based 
Interview Questions 
To answer a BDI question successfully, you need 
to tell a specific story, something that happened 
in the past. Using the S.O.A.R. formula will help 
you structure your answer effectively and tell a 
compelling story. The S.O.A.R. template: 
S = Situation 
Briefly describe the context within which 
you performed a task or faced a challenge. 
Be specific about when and where this 
occurred. 
O = Opportunity/Obstacle 
Explain what you had to overcome or how 
you made things better by articulating the 
idea, issue or defining the problem. 
A = Action 
Detail the specific actions you took to 
address the task or challenge. Focus on 
what you did personally, even if it was a 
team effort. What did you do in this 
situation? How did you solve the problem? 
What techniques or skills did you utilize? 
Include strong action words here like 
managed, initiated, developed, and 
analyzed. 
R = Results 
Share the outcomes or results of your 
actions. Highlight what you achieved and, if 
possible, quantify the results to show the 
impact of your actions (#, $, %). Many 
interviewees forget this part of their answer 
and it’s the most important part! 
Example of Using the SOAR method: 
Interviewer: "Can you give me an example of a 
time when you had to work as part of a team to 
achieve a goal?" 
Response: "Absolutely. Last semester, I was 
part of a team in my Organizational Behavior 
class where we had to complete a group 
project. The goal was to analyze a company's 
organizational structure and present 
recommendations for improvement. 
Situation: Our team of five was tasked with 
analyzing a mid-sized company's organizational 
structure and recommending improvements. 
The project had a tight deadline, and we had to 
present our findings to the class. 
Opportunity: As a team, we needed to gather 
data, analyze the company's structure, identify 
areas for improvement, and create a 
comprehensive presentation. My specific role 
was to lead the data analysis portion and 
ensure our recommendations were well-
supported by evidence.

What Are Illegal Interview Questions? 
Illegal interview questions are those that 
employers are not allowed to ask during an 
interview because they pertain to personal 
information that is not relevant to the job and 
can lead to discrimination. In Canada, these 
questions violate human rights laws that 
protect individuals from discrimination based 
on factors such as age, gender, marital status, 
religion, national origin, disability, and more. 
Examples of Illegal Interview Questions 
• Age: "How old are you?"
• Marital or Family Status: "Are you
married?" or "Do you have children?"
• Religion: "What is your religion?" or "Do
you observe any religious holidays?"
• Nationality or Ethnicity: "Where are you
from originally?" or "What is your
ethnicity?"
• Disability: "Do you have any disabilities?" or
"Have you ever filed a workers'
compensation claim?"
• Gender: "Do you plan to have children?" or
"How do you feel about working in a male-
dominated field?"
How to Respond to Illegal Interview 
Questions Professionally 
When faced with an illegal interview question, 
it's important to handle the situation 
professionally and tactfully. Here are a few 
strategies you can use. 
Redirect the Question: If asked, "Do you have 
children?" 
Response: "I’m fully committed to my 
professional responsibilities and managing my 
time effectively. I'm confident in my ability to 
meet the demands of this position." 
Seek Clarification: If asked, "Where are you 
from originally?" 
Response: "Could you clarify how my 
background is relevant to the responsibilities of 
this role? I’m excited to share how my skills and 
experience can contribute to your team." 
Address the Underlying Concern: If asked, "Do 
you plan to have children?" 
Response: "I assure you that I am dedicated to 
my career and capable of balancing personal 
and professional commitments. My focus is on 
contributing effectively to your organization." 
Politely Decline to Answer: If asked, "What is 
your religion?" 
Response: "I prefer to keep my personal beliefs 
private. However, I can assure you that my 
commitment to my work and my ability to 
contribute to your team are my top priorities." 
Turn It into a Job-Related Response: If asked, 
"How old are you?" 
Response: "I have over [X] years of experience 
in this industry, and I’m excited to bring my 
skills and knowledge to your organization."

uments: Have resumes,

2. One-on-One Interview is the most common
and traditional interview type where one

be a mix of interview questions including

tion!

TYPES OF INTERVIEW QUESTIONS
1. Behavioral Interview questions focus on how
the candidate has handled past situations. The
interviewer asks questions based on the
competencies required to do the job. These
questions assess your experience and are
based on the premise that past behavior is the
best predictor of future behavior.
Example: "Tell me about a time when you had
to lead a team under a tight deadline."
2. Situational Interview questions present
hypothetical situations that can occur on the job
and asks the applicant how they would handle
them. This type of interview question assesses
problem-solving and analytical skills.
Example: "What would you do if you were faced 
with an unhappy customer?" 
3. Techni
cal Interview questions assess specific
technical skills and knowledge related to the job.
Common in fields such as finance, actuary,

me through how you would use it to value a

the management consulting recruitment process.

challenges that a consultant might face.

PREPARATION IS THE KEY! 
Regardless of the type of interview or interview 
question, the first step to interview success is 
preparation. Good preparation enables you to: 
• Reduce interview anxiety
• A
ppear confident and professional
• Effectively market your qualifications
• Positively impress the interviewer(s)
How to prepare…
1. Understand the Organization
Find out as much as you can about the 
organization and its management by 
reviewing their website, following their social 
media, and connecting with people you may 
know who work there.

3 
What to look for… 
• What are the mission and values?
• What are their products and/or services,
and how are they marketed?
• What is their history, and what are their

other offices?
• What is their reputation?

Review the job posting to identify the key skills 
and qualifications they are looking for. Now, for

• What have I learned/gained from previous

Get Organized and Plan Ahead 
1. Prepare and practice answers to common
and behavioral interview questions. This
step is extremely important, the more you

There is more information about interview
questions starting on page 6. Remember,

2. Prepare your documents and portfolio with
the
 following:
• Extra copies of your resume.
• Examples o
f your work.

• Reference letter(s)
.

 of the job posting.

here:

e locations.

locati
ons.

our departure time so you arrive

4. Dress for Success!
•
•
Appearance counts - it’s part of your
first impression! This includes your
clothing, hair and grooming. Dress
conservatively in clothes that fit well,
have been recently cleaned and pressed.
No cologne, perfume or aftershave.
Many companies have “scent free
polices” to accommodate sensitivities.
• If you need to purchase an outfit,
consider
 it a worthwhile investment i n
your f
uture. You might b e able to find a

eal at a consignment or thrift

on
 you as a professional. Save some of
your 
shopping budget to have your

4 
• Bright colours and patterns can be

jackets, pants or skirts such as black,
grey, blue, beige or brown with a

5. Go wit
h the flow and be prepared for

t be late! If something happens, call

7. You
r interview starts even before you have

and polite to everyone you encounter, you

8. Tur
n your phone off and put it away! Take

At the Interview Make a Strong First 
Impression 
Int
roduce Yourself. Greet the interviewer 
warmly and confidently. A handshake, when 
appropriate, combined with a genuine smile, 
direct eye contact, and a clear “Thank you for 
seeing me” is a great way to launch the 
interview. If a handshake isn't customary or 
comfortable for you or the interviewer, a polite 
nod or verbal greeting works well too. Be sure 
to introduce yourself to everyone who is part of 
the interview process. To help you remember 
names, repeat their names back to them and/or 
write them down on the blank paper in your 
portfolio. This respectful and inclusive approach 
sets a positive tone for the interview. 
Good body language can help you feel and 
appear confident. Wait to be invited to sit, then 
sit tall with your shoulders back and try to avoid 
fidgeting. Be yourself and use natural hand 
gestures but avoid excessive movement. 
Maintain appropriate eye contact; looking 
directly at the interviewer when speaking or 
listening demonstrates engagement and 
confidence. 
However, be mindful that cultural differences 
and neurodivergence can affect body language 
and eye contact. For instance, in some 
Indigenous cultures, direct eye contact might be 
considered disrespectful or uncomfortable. 
Similarly, some neurodivergent individuals 
might find maintaining eye contact challenging. 
If this applies to you, focus on looking at the 
interviewer’s forehead or in their general 
direction rather than making direct eye contact. 
The key is to find a balance that shows you are 
attentive and engaged while respecting your 
cultural norms and personal comfort. 
Listen and respond carefully to the questions 
asked. Take a moment to think before you 
respond. Answer clearly and concisely. 
Remember, 38% of a first impression isn’t what 
we say, it’s how we say it and the tone of our 
voice. Be positive, never say anything negative 
about a previous employer, classmate or peer. 
Ask for clarification. To ensure you understand 
the question, don’t hesitate to ask for 
clarification or paraphrase the question to 
confirm your understanding. Take a brief

5 
moment to organize your thoughts before 
responding and use a structured approach like

and focused. Check in with the interviewer to 
ensure you’re addressing the question properly. 
Having your resume and a notepad in front of

experiences. 
Show Enthusiasm and Interest - express your 
interest in the role and the organization. 
Highlight your enthusiasm for the opportunities 
the position offers. 
Be Honest and Authentic - be yourself. Share 
your true experiences and strengths. Admit if 
you don’t know something and express your 
willingness to learn. 
Provide an answer to all questions! If they ask 
you a question that you have not experienced, 
do your very best to provide an example of a 
similar situation. If you don’t provide an answer 
they cannot evaluate or score you. Here’s an 
example “Tell me about a time a co-worker 
wasn’t contributing to the team. What did you 
do?” Perhaps you have not been in this exact 
situation with a co-worker, but you have been 
in this situation with a classmate on a group 
project or a teammate in your sports team. 
Always
 answer “Yes” to “Do you have any 
questions for us?” Asking well thought out 
questions demonstrates your sincere interest in 
the company and position, showing you’ve 
done your research. It’s also your chance to 
evaluate if the company is a good fit for you. 
Prepare four to six questions, as some may be 
answered during the interview. Have them 
printed out to ensure you remember them. 
Generally, stick to no more than three 
questions. Demonstrate your research by 
knowing the company’s mission, values, and 
recent achievements, and tailor your questions 
accordingly. 
See pag e 21 for a list of questions you may want 
to ask.

After the Interview: Next Steps 
1. Reflect o
n the interview, give yourself
feedback, and make notes of what you

2. Follow-up with the interviewer(s). Many

themselves, reiterate their skills and
interest in the job, show their appreciation
and mention anything they may have

6 
forgotten in the interview. Don’t be this

A typical follow-up is a thank you email sent 
within 24 hours of the interview. A 
handwritten card is also nice but should be 
dropped off in person to ensure it is 
received in a timely manner. Your email 
should include: 
• Thankin
g them for the interview
• Why you are a good fit
• Specifically, why you want to work for them
• Positive closing saying you look forward to
the opportunity to join their company
2. I hav
en’t heard back, what should I do?
One question you can ask at the end of the
interview is “When can I expect to hear

When you follow-up (through email or a

3. Asking
 for feedback creates a positive
impression and you might learn
something. Showing that you are open to
feedback and want to learn and improve
will add to your overall positive impression
and you might get some great insight that
will help you be successful in future
interviews. Some companies have policies
that don’t allow them to provide feedback,
or it might be very general, but it can’t hurt
to ask!
4. Netw
orking. Connect with the interviewer
and other company representatives on
LinkedIn, expressing your appreciation for
the opportunity. This can help keep you on
their radar and potentially open other
opportunities within the company.
5. Docum
enting Lessons Learned. Keep a
detailed record of your interview
experiences, including the questions asked,

This documentation will be a valuable

Use feedback and reflections to 
continuously improve your interview skills. 
Practice answering common questions,

By following these steps and thoroughly

TYPES OF INTERVIEW QUESTIONS
Common Questions & How to Answer 
Them 
These questions are used to determine your 
interests, motivations, goals, strengths, 
weaknesses and potential. You should have well 
prepared and tailored answers to these 
questions.

7 
Tell me about yourself.
This question helps the conversation get 
started. Provide the interviewer with a high-
level professional overview of who you are and 
how you are qualified for the position including 
your education, past relevant experience and 
extracurricular activities. Add in something 
unique about yourself to help them remember 
you. 
Tip: Don’t assume the person interviewing you 
has read your resume. 
What are your strengths? 
Keeping the position in mind, tell them about 
your strengths and provide relevant examples. 
Tip: Prove it! People tend to simply list a bunch 
of skills, which are meaningless without solid 
examples to demonstrate how you used them. 
What is your weakness? 
Select a weakness that is not a key competency 
related to the job and use this formula to 
demonstrate how you have improved: 
• W (weakn
ess) – tell them what it is, but
don’t spend too much time talking about it.
• A (actions) – explain the steps, ideally three,
you have taken to improve.
• R (results) – provide at least three positive
results that have come from your action
steps.
Tip: The
 recruiter cares more about your 
actions and results than your actual weakness. 
Sampl
e Answer: “If I had to choose a weakness 
it would be my public speaking skills. I wouldn’t 
describe myself as a natural born presenter. I 
recognize this and I have taken steps to improve 
by joining the Toastmasters Club at school, 
making time to practice when I give a 
presentation in class, as well as researching 
presentation techniques. As a result, I’m more 
confident and don’t shy away from presenting. 
My professor commented on my improvement, 
and I got an A on my last in-class presentation." 
What do you know about our company? 
Why are you interested in this position? 
Why should we hire you? 
These are very important questions that could 
have a significant impact on your interview 
results. Demonstrating that you have 
researched and understand the company will 
prove that you are sincerely interested in the 
role. These questions help the interviewer 
determine your “fit” within the 
team/organization. 
Tip: Tell the interviewer how your personal and 
professional values align with the company’s 
and what is going to motivate you to represent 
their company. 
Handling the "What is Your Salary 
Expectation?" Question 
One of the most challenging questions in a job 
interview is "What is your salary expectation?" 
It's important to approach this question with 
careful consideration, research, and tact. Here 
are some steps and tips to help you navigate 
this question confidently and professionally. 
1. Do Your Research
Before going to the interview, spend time 
researching salary ranges for the position you 
are applying for. Consider the following 
resources: 
• Online Salary Databases: Websites like
Glassdoor, PayScale, and LinkedIn Salary
can provide a range of salaries for specific
job titles and geographic locations.
• The Asper Employment Report available on
the website.
• Industry Reports: Professional associations
and industry reports often publish salary
surveys.
• Network: Talk to people in the industry,
including mentors, career services, and
alumni, to get a sense of typical salaries.

8 
• AI-Powered Salary Tools: Utilize AI tools
like Salary.com’s AI-driven salary predictor
or LinkedIn Salary Insights, which can
provide personalized salary estimates based
on your profile and job market trends.
2. Under
stand Your Value
Reflect on your skills, experience, and education 
to understand where you fit within the salary 
range you’ve researched. Consider: 
• Your Education: Advanced degrees or
certifications can justify higher salary
expectations.
• Relevant Experience: Internships, co-op
programs, and part-time jobs in your field
add value.
• Skills and Competencies: Specialized skills
or competencies can position you at the
higher end of the salary range.
3. Consider the Whole Compensation Package
Salary is just one part of the compensation 
package. Benefits, bonuses, stock options, and 
professional development opportunities also 
matter. When negotiating a salary, be prepared 
to consider other important benefits that add 
value to your compensation package: 
• Health Benefits
• Retirement Plans
• Paid Time Off
• Professional Development Opportunities
• Flexible Working Conditions
Prepare Your Answer 
You generally want to defer answering the 
salary question until you receive a job offer. 
The longer you can postpone providing a range, 
the more leverage you will have when it comes 
time to negotiate your salary – ideally when the 
employer has determined you are the best 
candidate and has offered you the position. 
When asked about salary expectations, you 
have several options for framing your response: 
• Deflect Initially: "I'm more interested in
finding a role that fits my skills and career
aspirations. I'm confident that if we
determine I'm the right fit, we can agree on
a fair salary.
• Turn the Question Around: "I'm flexible and
open to negotiation. Can you share the
budgeted salary range for this position?"
• Provide a Range: "Based on my research
and considering my experience and skills, I
believe a salary range of $X to $Y would be
appropriate. However, I'm open to
discussing this further."
Be Conf
ident and Professional. Your delivery is 
just as important as your answer. Keep these 
tips in mind: 
• Be Honest: Don’t inflate your expectations
unrealistically.
• Be Flexible: Show that you’re open to
negotiation.
• Be Positive: Frame your response in a way
that shows you’re motivated and interested
in the position and company.
Practicing your response can help you feel 
more confident and reduce anxiety. Consider 
answering the salary question by role playing 
with friends, family, or career services staff to 
refine your answer. 
Leveraging AI tools for Continued Practice 
Utilize AI tools like Interviewing.io or Big 
Interview, which use AI to simulate interview 
scenarios and provide feedback on your 
responses. These tools can help you practice 
your “salary expectation” responses in a 
realistic setting and help improve your delivery. 
By following these steps and tips, you'll be well-
prepared to handle the "What is your salary 
expectation?" question with confidence and

9 
professionalism. Remember, the goal is to find a 
mutually beneficial arrangement that reflects 
your value and fits within the employer’s 
budget. 
Behaviour Descriptive Interview 
Questions & How to Answer 
Behavioural-based or behaviour descriptive 
interview questions are designed to assess your 
past behavior in specific situations to predict 
your future performance in similar scenarios, 
using required competencies. These questions 
typically start with phrases like "Tell me about a 
time when..." or "Give an example of..." and 
focus on power/soft skills such as teamwork, 
problem-solving, leadership, and adaptability. 
Why Employers Use Behavioral-Based 
Interview Questions 
• To Predict Future Performance: Past
behavior is considered a reliable indicator of
future actions.
• To Evaluate Experience: Employers can
understand better how you have handled
real-life situations.
• To Assess Soft Skills: BDI questions help
interviewers gauge soft skills that are crucial
for job performance but not easily
measurable through technical questions.
How to Answer Behavioral-Based 
Interview Questions 
To answer a BDI question successfully, you need 
to tell a specific story, something that happened 
in the past. Using the S.O.A.R. formula will help 
you structure your answer effectively and tell a 
compelling story. The S.O.A.R. template: 
S = Situation 
Briefly describe the context within which 
you performed a task or faced a challenge. 
Be specific about when and where this 
occurred. 
O = Opportunity/Obstacle 
Explain what you had to overcome or how 
you made things better by articulating the 
idea, issue or defining the problem. 
A = Action 
Detail the specific actions you took to 
address the task or challenge. Focus on 
what you did personally, even if it was a 
team effort. What did you do in this 
situation? How did you solve the problem? 
What techniques or skills did you utilize? 
Include strong action words here like 
managed, initiated, developed, and 
analyzed. 
R = Results 
Share the outcomes or results of your 
actions. Highlight what you achieved and, if 
possible, quantify the results to show the 
impact of your actions (#, $, %). Many 
interviewees forget this part of their answer 
and it’s the most important part! 
Example of Using the SOAR method: 
Interviewer: "Can you give me an example of a 
time when you had to work as part of a team to 
achieve a goal?" 
Response: "Absolutely. Last semester, I was 
part of a team in my Organizational Behavior 
class where we had to complete a group 
project. The goal was to analyze a company's 
organizational structure and present 
recommendations for improvement. 
Situation: Our team of five was tasked with 
analyzing a mid-sized company's organizational 
structure and recommending improvements. 
The project had a tight deadline, and we had to 
present our findings to the class. 
Opportunity: As a team, we needed to gather 
data, analyze the company's structure, identify 
areas for improvement, and create a 
comprehensive presentation. My specific role 
was to lead the data analysis portion and 
ensure our recommendations were well-
supported by evidence.

10 
Action: First, I organized an initial meeting to 
discuss our strategy and divide tasks based on 
each member's strengths. I took the initiative to 
set up a shared document where we could all 
contribute our findings and track our progress. I 
then focused on gathering data from various 
sources, including the company’s annual 
reports, employee surveys, and industry 
benchmarks. 
I ensured open communication by scheduling 
regular check-ins and encouraging team 
members to share updates. When we 
encountered conflicting opinions on some 
recommendations, I facilitated a discussion to 
weigh the pros and cons, helping the team 
reach a consensus. 
Result: As a result, we were able to deliver a 
thorough and well-organized presentation on 
time. Our analysis was praised for its depth and 
accuracy, and we received an 'A' for the project. 
Additionally, the collaborative approach I 
encouraged helped us work efficiently and 
strengthened our team dynamics. This 
experience taught me the importance of clear 
communication, organization, and the value of 
leveraging each team member's strengths to 
achieve a common goal." 
This response effectively uses the SOAR method 
(Situation, Opportunity/Obstacle, Action, 
Result) to structure the answer, demonstrating 
this student’s teamwork, leadership, 
communication, and organizational skills. 
Examples of BDI Questions 
Interviewers design BDI questions to allow 
candidates to share stories highlighting 
competencies required to be successful in the 
role. Examples of BDI questions and the 
competency required below: 
Compete
ncy: Stress management 
• Tell me about a difficult situation when it
was desirable for you to keep a positive
attitude. What did you do?
Compete
ncy: Time management 
• Tell me about a time you had to handle
multiple responsibilities. How did you
organize the work you needed to do?
Compete
ncy: Teamwork 
• Tell me about a time when you were
working as part of a team and one of the
members wasn’t contributing. What did
you do?
Compet
ency: Customer focus 
• Tell me about a time when you had to
handle a difficult customer. What did you
do?
Tip: The
 emphasis of your answer (or story) 
should be on your actions and results. Think 
about providing three actions and three results 
for a complete story. So, the formula would 
look like this S.O.A.A.A.R.R.R. 
Other Types of Questions 
In addition to behavioral-based questions, 
interviewers may use various other types of 
questions to assess different aspects of a 
candidate's fit for a role. Here are some 
additional types of interview questions and 
examples of each: 
1. Traditional Interview Questions
These questions are straightforward and focus 
on your background, experience, and general

Illegal Interview Questions and How to 
Respond to Them 
What Are Illegal Interview Questions? 
Illegal interview questions are those that 
employers are not allowed to ask during an 
interview because they pertain to personal 
information that is not relevant to the job and 
can lead to discrimination. In Canada, these 
questions violate human rights laws that 
protect individuals from discrimination based 
on factors such as age, gender, marital status, 
religion, national origin, disability, and more. 
Examples of Illegal Interview Questions 
• Age: "How old are you?"
• Marital or Family Status: "Are you
married?" or "Do you have children?"
• Religion: "What is your religion?" or "Do
you observe any religious holidays?"
• Nationality or Ethnicity: "Where are you
from originally?" or "What is your
ethnicity?"
• Disability: "Do you have any disabilities?" or
"Have you ever filed a workers'
compensation claim?"
• Gender: "Do you plan to have children?" or
"How do you feel about working in a male-
dominated field?"
How to Respond to Illegal Interview 
Questions Professionally 
When faced with an illegal interview question, 
it's important to handle the situation 
professionally and tactfully. Here are a few 
strategies you can use. 
Redirect the Question: If asked, "Do you have 
children?" 
Response: "I’m fully committed to my 
professional responsibilities and managing my 
time effectively. I'm confident in my ability to 
meet the demands of this position." 
Seek Clarification: If asked, "Where are you 
from originally?" 
Response: "Could you clarify how my 
background is relevant to the responsibilities of 
this role? I’m excited to share how my skills and 
experience can contribute to your team." 
Address the Underlying Concern: If asked, "Do 
you plan to have children?" 
Response: "I assure you that I am dedicated to 
my career and capable of balancing personal 
and professional commitments. My focus is on 
contributing effectively to your organization." 
Politely Decline to Answer: If asked, "What is 
your religion?" 
Response: "I prefer to keep my personal beliefs 
private. However, I can assure you that my 
commitment to my work and my ability to 
contribute to your team are my top priorities." 
Turn It into a Job-Related Response: If asked, 
"How old are you?" 
Response: "I have over [X] years of experience 
in this industry, and I’m excited to bring my 
skills and knowledge to your organization."

Tips for Handling Illegal Questions 
• Stay Calm and Professional: It’s important
to maintain your composure and respond
politely, even if the question makes you
uncomfortable.
• Focus on the Job: Try to steer the
conversation back to your qualifications,
experience, and how you can contribute to
the role.
• Know Your Rights: Be aware of your legal
rights and the types of questions that are
not permissible. If necessary, you can report
the incident to the appropriate authorities
after the interview.
By preparing for the possibility of illegal 
questions and knowing how to respond to them 
professionally, you can navigate these situations 
with confidence and maintain a positive 
impression during your interview.

chunks.text: ## Page 1 INTERVIEW GUIDE CAREER DEVELOPMENT CENTRE BComm. ## Page 2 1 Interview Guide Congratulations, You Got the Interview! Getting an i nterview is a significant achievement. Your resume and cover letter have successfully showcased your qualifications, impressing the prospective employer enough to want to meet you in person (or virtually). Now, it's your chance to confirm your skills and abilities, demonstrate your fit for the role, and learn more about the role and the company. This interview is not only an opportunity for them to get to know you better but also for you to expand on your resume, present your strengths confidently, and evaluate if this position and organization are the right match for your career aspirations. Prepare well, stay positive, and make the most of this exciting opportunity – you’re already off to a great start! Top 10 Tips for a Successful Interview 1. Understand the role: Know the key responsibilities and skills required. 2. Research the company: Understand its mission, values, and recent news. How do your personal and professional values align with the organization’s? 3. Prepare answers using the SOAR method to possible questions (p9); share your stories - experience, skills and accomplishments. 4. Anticipate responses to common questions. 5. Develop thoughtful questions about the role and company. 6. Dress appropriately: Choose professional attire. 7. Practice: Conduct mock interviews with CDC career advisors. Record yourself using technology. 8. Plan your journey: For in person interviews, arrive early (10 min). If virtual, test technology and set up (lighting/sound). 9. Bring doc uments: Have resumes, references, and a notepad. 10. Follow up: Send a thank-you email and reflect on your performance. DIFFERENT INTERVIEW TYPES & FORMATS 1. Pre-screening Interview (virtual/phone) The first interview. Commonly used to pre- screen applicants before an in-person interview is scheduled or when the candidate and employer are not located in the same city. Telephone Interview tips • Find a quiet location: Minimize background noise. • Prepare notes: Have your key points and resume at hand. • Practice speaking clearly: Ensure clarity and pace. • Listen actively: Don’t interrupt and respond thoughtfully. • Smile: It reflects in your voice. Video Interview tips • Test technology - ensure a stable Wi-Fi connection, working camera and microphone and fully charged device. • Choose a quiet, well-lit space with a professional background. • Dress like you would for an in-person interview. • Maintain eye contact - look at the camera, not the screen and remember to smile. • Prepare notes - have your key points and resume at hand. • Minimize distractions - silence notifications. ## Page 3 2 2. One-on-One Interview is the most common and traditional interview type where one interviewer meets with one candidate. Can be a mix of interview questions including behavioral, situational, or conversational depending on the skill of the interviewer. 3. Panel Interview involves two or more interviewers from different areas of the organization usually taking turns asking questions. Each interviewer may focus on different aspects of the candidate’s skills and experience. 4. Group Interview is when multiple candidates are interviewed simultaneously. This format assesses teamwork, communication skills, and how candidates perform in group settings. Questions can involve group tasks or individual responses in a group setting.

Behavioral Interview questions focus on how the candidate has handled past situations. The interviewer asks questions based on the competencies required to do the job. These questions assess your experience and are based on the premise that past behavior is the best predictor of future behavior. Example: "Tell me about a time when you had to lead a team under a tight deadline." 2. Situational Interview questions present hypothetical situations that can occur on the job and asks the applicant how they would handle them. This type of interview question assesses problem-solving and analytical skills. Example: "What would you do if you were faced with an unhappy customer?" 3. Techni cal Interview questions assess specific technical skills and knowledge related to the job. Common in fields such as finance, actuary, accounting, data analytics. Example: "Can you explain the concept of discounted cash flow (DCF) analysis and walk me through how you would use it to value a company.” 4. Case interview questions are a critical part of the management consulting recruitment process. The primary goal is to assess the candidate's problem-solving skills, analytical abilities, and how they would approach real-world business challenges that a consultant might face. Example: "A client’s sales have dropped by 20% over the past year. How would you investigate and address this issue?" PREPARATION IS THE KEY! A handshake, when appropriate, combined with a genuine smile, direct eye contact, and a clear “Thank you for seeing me” is a great way to launch the interview. If a handshake isn't customary or comfortable for you or the interviewer, a polite nod or verbal greeting works well too. Be sure to introduce yourself to everyone who is part of the interview process. To help you remember names, repeat their names back to them and/or write them down on the blank paper in your portfolio. This respectful and inclusive approach sets a positive tone for the interview. Good body language can help you feel and appear confident. Wait to be invited to sit, then sit tall with your shoulders back and try to avoid fidgeting. Be yourself and use natural hand gestures but avoid excessive movement. Maintain appropriate eye contact; looking directly at the interviewer when speaking or listening demonstrates engagement and confidence. However, be mindful that cultural differences and neurodivergence can affect body language and eye contact. Similarly, some neurodivergent individuals might find maintaining eye contact challenging. If this applies to you, focus on looking at the interviewer’s forehead or in their general direction rather than making direct eye contact. The key is to find a balance that shows you are attentive and engaged while respecting your cultural norms and personal comfort. Listen and respond carefully to the questions asked. Behaviour Descriptive Interview Questions & How to Answer Behavioural-based or behaviour descriptive interview questions are designed to assess your past behavior in specific situations to predict your future performance in similar scenarios, using required competencies. These questions typically start with phrases like "Tell me about a time when..." or "Give an example of..." and focus on power/soft skills such as teamwork, problem-solving, leadership, and adaptability. Why Employers Use Behavioral-Based Interview Questions • To Predict Future Performance: Past behavior is considered a reliable indicator of future actions. • To Evaluate Experience: Employers can understand better how you have handled real-life situations. • To Assess Soft Skills: BDI questions help interviewers gauge soft skills that are crucial for job performance but not easily measurable through technical questions. How to Answer Behavioral-Based Interview Questions To answer a BDI question successfully, you need to tell a specific story, something that happened in the past. Using the S.O.A.R. formula will help you structure your answer effectively and tell a compelling story. The S.O.A.R. template: S = Situation Briefly describe the context within which you performed a task or faced a challenge. Be specific about when and where this occurred. O = Opportunity/Obstacle Explain what you had to overcome or how you made things better by articulating the idea, issue or defining the problem. A = Action Detail the specific actions you took to address the task or challenge. Focus on what you did personally, even if it was a team effort. What did you do in this situation? How did you solve the problem? What techniques or skills did you utilize? Include strong action words here like managed, initiated, developed, and analyzed. R = Results Share the outcomes or results of your actions. Highlight what you achieved and, if possible, quantify the results to show the impact of your actions (#, $, %). Many interviewees forget this part of their answer and it’s the most important part! Illegal Interview Questions and How to Respond to Them What Are Illegal Interview Questions? Illegal interview questions are those that employers are not allowed to ask during an interview because they pertain to personal information that is not relevant to the job and can lead to discrimination. In Canada, these questions violate human rights laws that protect individuals from discrimination based on factors such as age, gender, marital status, religion, national origin, disability, and more. Examples of Illegal Interview Questions • Age: "How old are you?" • Marital or Family Status: "Are you married?" or "Do you have children?" • Religion: "What is your religion?" or "Do you observe any religious holidays?" • Nationality or Ethnicity: "Where are you from originally?" or "What is your ethnicity?" • Disability: "Do you have any disabilities?" or "Have you ever filed a workers' compensation claim?" • Gender: "Do you plan to have children?" or "How do you feel about working in a male- dominated field?" How to Respond to Illegal Interview Questions Professionally When faced with an illegal interview question, it's important to handle the situation professionally and tactfully. Here are a few strategies you can use. Redirect the Question: If asked, "Do you have children?" Response: "I’m fully committed to my professional responsibilities and managing my time effectively. Response: "Could you clarify how my background is relevant to the responsibilities of this role? I’m excited to share how my skills and experience can contribute to your team." Address the Underlying Concern: If asked, "Do you plan to have children?" Response: "I assure you that I am dedicated to my career and capable of balancing personal and professional commitments.
